title: Leadership as an art form
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez argues that leaders keep falling short despite feedback and coaching because they have accepted a narrow, transactional definition of leadership as control, output and a line in a job description. Her counter-claim is that leadership is human and artistic work, a craft requiring patience, presence, self-awareness and honesty. She extends the metaphor into a working image: every late email, unprepared meeting, unwritten policy and evaded hard truth is a brushstroke that together paints the culture people live in. The practical move is accountability, owning one's strokes and being willing to start over with a new palette. She ends with a self-check question about what kind of piece the leader is trying to create.
points: Leaders often fail not from incompetence but from treating leadership as a title or checklist item rather than as creative, human work.
The brushstroke image makes culture the cumulative result of small actions and omissions, including silence in the face of harm.
Good leaders, like artists, think about their impact beyond the immediate product and beyond their own tenure.
The piece asks leaders to own their strokes and, where needed, restart with a new approach instead of defending the existing canvas.
quotes: Leadership isn’t just a job. It’s not just a title. And it’s certainly not a box to simply be checked and moved on from.
Leadership is, fundamentally, something creative. It’s emotional, powerful, and evocative. It requires not only skill, but patience, presence, self-awareness, heart, soul, and honesty.

Good leaders, like good artists, are thinking beyond the mere products of their work, but on the impact they may have even when they’re gone. And this idea of just winging it? Without consideration of what’s next? That’s not the move.
On the flip side, every single thing impacts something else. Think of every action and inaction as a brushstroke that paves the way for what comes next—the good, the bad, and everything in between.
Before we know it, we're all standing in front of a big, confusing—sometimes even ugly—canvas. And guess what? We were there. We helped paint it.

We need to own our strokes, clean up our spills, and sometimes, we even need to start over with a new color palette. Leadership is art, and art is messy, layered, honest, and human. And when done well, it can transform not just a team—but an entire system.
